name: Cercospora leaf spot
summary: A Cannabis leaf-spot disease that often begins on older lower leaves as yellow flecks and develops into round lesions with pale centers, dark borders, and yellow halos. Conidiophore and laboratory evidence are needed because several pathogens make similar spots.
indicators: Small yellow flecks appear first on older lower foliage
Lesions become round, approximately 2 to 6 mm, with tan-to-white centers
Dark brown to purplish raised borders and yellow halos may develop
Melanized conidiophores can become visible in lesion centers
exclusions: Dark pycnidia support Septoria
Sooty underside masses support Pseudocercospora
Shot-hole lesions with Colletotrichum evidence support anthracnose
Laboratory testing identifies another pathogen

progression.description: Small yellow flecks appear on older lower leaves.
Round lesions enlarge and centers pale while dark borders and halos become clearer.
Spots can coalesce and lesion centers may break down.

confirmation: Inspect lesion centers with magnification and submit tissue for fungal identification.
Use morphology and/or molecular testing before assigning Cercospora cf. flagellaris at species level.
immediateActions: Document early lower-canopy distribution and preserve representative lesions.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed leaf-spot disease management and sanitation appropriate to the setting.
prevention: Scout older foliage and reduce avoidable leaf wetness.
Avoid moving symptomatic material into clean areas.
warnings: Round pale-centered lesions are not unique to Cercospora.
Cercospora often appears as part of a multi-pathogen field leaf-spot complex.

sources.title: First Report of Cercospora cf. flagellaris on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Cercospora leaf spot began on older lower-canopy hemp leaves as small yellow flecks and progressed to round 2 to 6 mm lesions with tan-to-white centers, dark brown-to-purplish borders, and yellow halos.
Melanized conidiophores could become visible in lesion centers before centers disintegrated.
Whole-plant inoculation reproduced similar symptoms and the fungus was recovered again, supporting pathogenicity rather than visual association alone.

sources.title: Leaf Spot Disease Development and Its Effect on Yield of Essential Oil-Producing Hemp Cultivars in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Two Kentucky field experiments in 2020 and 2021 evaluated Bipolaris, Cercospora, and Septoria leaf spots across four essential-oil hemp cultivar groups.
In those experiments Bipolaris was first observed seven to eight weeks after planting and increased through the end of the season; this is a study observation, not a universal onset rule.
All three evaluated leaf spots were more severe in the middle canopy than the upper canopy, and susceptibility differed among cultivar groups; neither pattern is a universal diagnostic threshold.
Reported yield associations concerned the combined leaf-spot disease complex under the tested cultivars, sites, and seasons and must not be attributed to Bipolaris alone.
Overlapping leaf-spot syndromes mean paired canopy observations, temporal follow-up, fungal morphology, culture, and molecular diagnostics are more reliable than one lesion photograph.

name: Exserohilum / Helminthosporium leaf blight
summary: A laboratory-supported Cannabis leaf, stem, and flower blight reported across several North Carolina industrial-hemp cultivars. Small round lesions with dark-brown margins and gray-brown aging centers are compatible, especially when pepper-like conidia appear, but the pattern overlaps multiple hemp leaf spots and requires plant-linked fungal identification.
stages: fiber, seed, and flower production in the original report
field production; greenhouse transfer not established
indicators: Small round lesions begin brown and may darken toward brown-black while retaining a distinctly dark-brown margin
Lesion centers age to gray-brown, creating a darker-border and paler-center pattern
Fine dark pepper-like sporulation can become visible within gray-brown lesion centers as lesions age
Multiple nearby spots may merge into larger irregular necrotic areas rather than remaining discrete circles
Compatible lesions or blight occur on leaves and may also be documented on stems or flowers of the same plant
Abundant pigmented, septate Exserohilum-compatible conidia are recovered from fresh plant-linked lesions
ITS1 plus RPB2 sequence evidence supports E. rostratum rather than relying on a broad historical â€œHelminthosporiumâ€ label
The image or video sequence retains whole-plant distribution, both leaf surfaces, lesion scale, and the exact sampled lesion linked to the laboratory result
exclusions: Angular lesions constrained by major veins, bacterial streaming or ooze, and bacterial isolation support a bacterial leaf-spot differential
Black pinhead pycnidia in tan lesions beginning on older lower foliage support Septoria rather than pepper-like Exserohilum conidia
Yellow flecks expanding to pale tan or white centers with a yellow halo and Cercospora-compatible structures support Cercospora
Dark gray or black fuzzy sporulation on both leaf surfaces with Bipolaris identification supports Bipolaris leaf spot
Purplish-gray downy growth on the leaf underside opposite upper-surface chlorosis or necrosis supports downy mildew
Fusarium culture or molecular evidence and compatible foliar, flower, stem-canker, or wilt findings support a Fusarium disease
A sharp spray, contact, abrasion, or field-edge exposure pattern occurs without fungal structures or plant-linked organism evidence
Only a detached, low-resolution, single-surface spot image is available without plant identity, progression, scale, or sample linkage

progression.description: Small round brown lesions become visible; the evidence does not establish a dependable first-affected leaf age or canopy position, so record both rather than infer them.
Centers become gray-brown while margins remain dark brown, increasing the target-like contrast but not making the lesion species-specific.
Fine dark pepper-like conidia may appear in aging centers; capture a macro view and microscopy from the same lesion.
Adjacent circular spots merge into larger irregular necrotic regions, obscuring the early round morphology.
Leaf burden increases and compatible blight may also occur on stems or flowers; cultivar, organ sequence, rate, and severity are not universalized from the North Carolina reports.

confirmation: Capture the intact plant and canopy distribution, then photograph affected organs, both leaf surfaces, lesion scale, center and margin, and any stem or flower lesions before sampling.
Record plant identity, cultivar, production purpose, stage, location, date, recent weather or leaf wetness, irrigation splash, sprays, and whether spots are expanding or coalescing over time.
Collect several fresh active lesion margins under the same identifiers as the images; retain matched apparently healthy tissue and avoid relying only on dry late-stage centers.
Examine lesion scrapings or cultures microscopically for pigmented septate conidia with Exserohilum-compatible morphology; â€œpepper-likeâ€ appearance in a photograph is not microscopy.
Use culture plus multilocus or otherwise validated molecular identification; the Cannabis reports used ITS1 and RPB2 evidence for E. rostratum.
Investigate bacterial streaming/ooze, pycnidia, opposite-surface growth, other fungal structures, and mixed recovery because hemp leaf spots overlap and coinfection is possible.

Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf, single-surface, low-resolution, culture-unlinked, ITS-only, mixed-organism, stock, forum, vendor, or generated captures out of the confirmed class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Preserve fresh plant-linked lesions before treatment or disposal and separate strongly affected material from clean handling routes.
Avoid moving wet symptomatic foliage or contaminated debris through clean areas; inspect leaves, stems, and flowers together.
Measure and document leaf-wetness and splash conditions while retaining the differential diagnosis; environment is context, not organism proof.
correctivePlan: Base pathogen-specific action on a qualified plant-diagnostic result and locally applicable crop rules.
If prolonged leaf wetness, dense airflow restriction, weeds, or infected debris are documented, correct those risks without treating response to correction as proof of E. rostratum.
prevention: Scout multiple canopy positions and plant organs with repeat photography so early round spots, aging centers, sporulation, and coalescence are not reconstructed from unrelated images.
Reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness and splash, improve canopy airflow where practical, and manage infected crop debris and weedy grass hosts according to local guidance.
Maintain plant, cultivar, lot, location, date, image, and diagnostic-sample identifiers through the laboratory workflow.
warnings: â€œHelminthosporiumâ€ is a historical/common disease name and does not by itself identify the modern fungal taxon.
Dark-bordered round spots, gray-brown centers, pepper-like dots, coalescence, and blight are not independently species-specific.

The available Cannabis evidence does not establish a universal first-affected leaf age, canopy location, incubation period, progression rate, cultivar susceptibility, incidence threshold, or yield effect.
A visually compatible image without plant-linked morphology and molecular evidence is a low-confidence differential, not ground truth.
The NC State image has no item-level reusable license or linked laboratory record on the landing page and remains metadata-only, hidden, training-prohibited, and subject to human review.

sources.title: First Report of Exserohilum rostratum Causing Foliar Blight of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa)
supportedClaims: During the 2017 and 2018 North Carolina growing seasons, several industrial-hemp cultivars grown for fiber, seed, and flower showed foliar, stem, and floral blight, establishing a multi-organ Cannabis disease context rather than a generic non-host transfer.
Compatible hemp lesions were round and brown to black with dark margins and contained abundant conidia; lesion appearance alone was not the basis for the organism label.

The report is geographically and temporally bounded to sampled North Carolina production in 2017â€“2018 and does not establish a universal leaf-age order, canopy-position sequence, cultivar response, incidence threshold, or severity scale.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017â€“2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

The survey documented Serratia-associated, vein-limited angular hemp lesions and red bacterial ooze emerging from punctured lesions, while emphasizing that hemp leaf diseases overlap visually and require diagnostic separation.

sources.title: Exserohilum Leaf Spot Causing Problems in NC Hemp
supportedClaims: NC State Extension identifies Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot on multiple industrial-hemp strains in North Carolina and warns that other hemp leaf spots can look similar, so accurate diagnosis is important.
The institutional hemp description states that Exserohilum can affect leaves, stems, and flowers; leaf lesions are most distinct as small round spots with dark-brown margins and gray-brown centers.
As lesions age, spores may appear in gray-brown centers like fine ground pepper and lesions may coalesce into larger irregular necrotic areas; these are progression cues, not species confirmation.
The page names bacterial, Fusarium, and Septoria leaf spots as similar hemp diseases and characterizes bacterial leaf spot/blight as angular, supporting explicit differential checks.

NC State Extension states that hemp leaf spots can look similar and accurate diagnosis is important; its industrial-hemp bacterial leaf spot/blight reference is characterized only as angular lesions and is not presented as species-confirmed Serratia ground truth.

The same institutional differential describes Exserohilum lesions as small, round spots with dark-brown margins and gray-brown centers that may develop pepper-like spores as they age, helping separate a fungal leaf-spot pattern from vein-limited bacterial-compatible injury.
The page identifies bacterial, Fusarium, and Septoria leaf spots as visual alternatives to Exserohilum, supporting a multi-pathogen differential rather than an image-only bacterial species label.

name: Fusarium foliar, flower and head blight complex
summary: A Cannabis Fusarium disease complex affecting leaves, flowers, drying floral material, stems and grain heads. It must be separated from Fusarium root/crown rot because infection site, symptom pattern and confirmation evidence differ.
indicators: Floral surfaces develop abundant hyphae with light-brown necrotic tips
Leaves develop roughly circular light-brown lesions with darker brown margins and gray-brown aging centers
Blight is centered on floral/head tissue rather than beginning as root decay
Fusarium macroconidia, culture, sequence or species-specific molecular evidence accompanies compatible tissue
exclusions: Root/crown rot and vascular wilt dominate without foliar or floral lesions
Gray fuzzy sporulation and diagnostic evidence identify Botrytis
White mold and sclerotia identify a Sclerotinia or southern-blight differential
No Fusarium evidence is present and drying/heat/mechanical injury explains floral browning

progression.description: Localized leaf lesions or necrotic flower tips develop and surface hyphae may become visible.
Necrosis expands through affected foliar or floral tissue.
F. graminearum may be detectable before obvious blight, especially around flowering, so visual absence is not proof of absence.

confirmation: Submit representative fresh lesion/flower tissue for culture and molecular identification when Fusarium species matters.
For suspected F. graminearum, species-specific molecular assays can detect infection that is not yet visually obvious.
immediateActions: Separate suspect floral material from clean material and preserve diagnostic samples before treatment or disposal.
Inspect roots/crowns separately so root Fusarium is not conflated with foliar/flower blight.
correctivePlan: Use laboratory-supported disease management and sanitation appropriate to the production stage and local crop rules.
prevention: Use clean propagation/seed sources where applicable and reduce movement of symptomatic plant debris.
Track humidity, rainfall/leaf wetness, and flower-stage disease development without treating environment as proof of pathogen identity.
warnings: Fusarium flower browning is not visually species-specific.
The 2020 survey identified both F. equiseti and F. graminearum in the foliar/flower blight complex; do not collapse every lesion into F. graminearum.
Image-only absence cannot exclude latent F. graminearum infection.

name: Powdery mildew
scientificName: Golovinomyces ambrosiae / Podosphaera macularis complex on Cannabis sativa
summary: Cannabis powdery mildew is a disease class marked by superficial whitish mycelium and conidia that expand across living foliage and sometimes stems or flowers. The phenotype can strongly support powdery mildew, but images cannot distinguish the documented Cannabis pathogens Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis.
indicators: Small whitish, powdery, superficial colonies occur on either leaf surface; colony texture sits on the tissue rather than appearing only as internal chlorosis.
Colonies enlarge and coalesce, producing irregular white coverage that may spread among leaves, petioles, and stems; susceptible plants can show extensive surface mycelium and conidia.
Under severe adult-plant pressure, white colonies can extend onto sugar leaves, petioles, stem tissue, flower bracts, or buds.
Affected leaves can lose vigor, yellow, become necrotic, or defoliate as disease severity increases, but these secondary changes are nonspecific.
No universal leaf-age onset is established: capture the oldest, newest, upper, lower, interior, and exterior symptomatic and apparently clean foliage rather than assuming a nutrient-mobility pattern.

Powdery-mildew colonies may become visible within roughly one week under favorable conditions, while one controlled Cannabis experiment reported susceptible leaf and stem colonies within 45 days of germination under continuous inoculum pressure.
exclusions: Foliar spray or mineral residue often follows droplet edges or application patterns, may occur on nonliving surfaces, and lacks hyphae, conidiophores, and an advancing colony margin.
Normal glandular trichomes are regularly distributed structures anchored to floral tissue rather than irregular spreading white mycelial patches.
Spider-mite silk forms threads or sheets associated with mites, eggs, cast skins, and feeding stippling rather than a powdery fungal colony.
Botrytis produces advancing brown or water-soaked flower decay and gray-brown sporulation, often including internal tissue breakdown, rather than only superficial white colonies.
Downy mildew is associated with angular chlorotic-to-necrotic lesions and corresponding gray-to-purplish underside sporulation under wet or humid conditions.
Leaf bleaching, variegation, nutrient chlorosis, and camera overexposure remain within tissue and do not resolve into fungal hyphae and conidia under magnification.

progression.description: A clean image is symptom-negative only; resistant genotypes can suppress visible colonization, and visually clean tissue is not a universal pathogen-negative control.
Few small superficial white colonies appear. In the PM2 study scale, grade 1 represented restricted, nonspreading colonies covering less than 25% of the leaf.
Colonies enlarge and merge. Study grades 2 and 3 represented 25â€“50% and 50â€“75% leaf-area coverage.
Study grade 4 represented 75â€“100% leaf coverage; petioles, stems, sugar leaves, bracts, or buds may also be colonized under severe adult-plant pressure.
Leaves may yellow, become necrotic, or defoliate, and flower quality can decline; these effects require the active colony to preserve the powdery-mildew label.

lookAlikes: Botrytis gray mold or bud rot
confirmation: Do not assign a powdery-mildew species from a photograph or video. Capture whole-canopy distribution plus sharp upper- and lower-surface macros from several symptomatic and adjacent apparently clean leaves.

At the active colony edge, use magnification to document superficial hyphae and chains of conidia; include a scale and a gentle side-lit video or focus stack that separates fungal growth from residue and trichomes.
Record whether material transfers when touched, but do not use wipe behavior alone as confirmation because residue and fungal spores can both move.

For organism-level ground truth, submit fresh tissue to a qualified plant diagnostic laboratory for microscopy and molecular testing; both Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis are documented on hemp.

Record cultivar or genotype, plant age, growth stage, organ, canopy position, production setting, first-observed date, repeated fixed-area coverage, temperature, humidity, and recent foliar applications.
Treat absent colonies as a symptom-negative observation, not proof of resistance or pathogen absence; controlled resistance claims require replicated inoculation and appropriate susceptible controls.
immediateActions: Separate or flag affected plants, minimize handling and airflow disturbances that can disperse conidia, and preserve a fresh diagnostic sample before removal.
Map affected plants and organs, capture pre-intervention colony coverage, and inspect nearby plants on both leaf surfaces and flower-adjacent tissue.
correctivePlan: Use only legal, crop-, site-, and growth-stage-appropriate disease management selected for the production system; follow the product label and local testing requirements.
Remove heavily affected material without dispersing spores where permitted, clean tools and contact surfaces, and track new colony development rather than persistent old discoloration.
Review humidity, air movement, canopy density, intake material, and cross-room movement as epidemiological context without treating any single environmental reading as diagnostic proof.
prevention: Inspect incoming plants and clones under magnification and maintain cultivar/source identity so repeated susceptibility can be recognized.
Scout fixed leaves and flower-adjacent tissues across canopy zones, recording new colony area over time and retaining source-group identity for image sequences.
warnings: The 2019 Kentucky DOI originally identified Golovinomyces spadiceus; later taxonomy generally includes that name within G. ambrosiae. Preserve the original title and do not silently rewrite historical species labels.
At least two powdery-mildew fungi, Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis, have been PCR-confirmed on hemp, so disease-class imagery is not species-level ground truth.
The PM2 0-to-4 leaf-coverage scale is a controlled resistance-study scale, not a universal field severity, yield-loss, or intervention threshold.

Cultivar, genotype, pathogen isolate, organ, plant stage, and inoculum pressure can change visible severity; adult plants in one study sometimes appeared more susceptible than their earlier clone assay.
The linked CC BY 4.0 susceptible-versus-resistant Figure 2 is a shared-experiment composite. It remains training-ineligible, and the resistant panel is not an independent universal negative sample.
Do not consume visibly mold-contaminated material, and do not apply unapproved products to Cannabis or flowering tissue.

sources.title: First Report of Powdery Mildew Caused by Golovinomyces spadiceus on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: The Kentucky report identified a powdery mildew on industrial hemp as Golovinomyces spadiceus using fungal morphology and ITS plus 28S sequence evidence.
The historical G. spadiceus name in this report is now generally treated within the amended G. ambrosiae concept; the DOI must not be cited as though its original title named G. ambrosiae.

sources.title: Characterization of Powdery Mildew Fungi Affecting Hemp in the Pacific Northwest
supportedClaims: Surveys of 74 hemp fields in Oregon and Washington across three time points in 2021 and 2022 found powdery mildew later in the season in Oregon but not at the early survey point.
Diagnostic PCR detected both Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis on hemp, so a white powdery-mildew phenotype does not resolve the causal species.
Among assayed survey samples, G. ambrosiae was much more frequent than P. macularis, but the regional and seasonal sample does not establish a universal species prior for other production systems.

sources.title: Discovery and Genetic Mapping of PM1, a Powdery Mildew Resistance Gene in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Patchy white mycelial colonies developed on Cannabis foliage and flowers and were associated with reduced vigor, but colony presence did not by itself identify every possible powdery-mildew species.

In two segregating Cannabis populations, susceptible plants developed white colonies on leaves and stems within 45 days of germination under continuous inoculum pressure, while PM1-bearing plants showed complete resistance to the tested Pacific Northwest G. ambrosiae isolate.

Plants were followed through flowering, and 55 clonal replicates were reinfected to validate scores; resistance or absence of visible colonies in this experiment is genotype- and isolate-specific rather than a universal negative control.

Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 susceptible-versus-resistant Cannabis comparison; its panels share experimental source context and must not be treated as independent training samples without source grouping and review.

sources.title: Mapping and Characterization of a Novel Powdery Mildew Resistance Locus (PM2) in Cannabis sativa L.
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Seifi et al.)
supportedClaims: The study used a leaf-area severity scale of 0 for no symptoms, 1 for less than 25% coverage with few restricted nonspreading colonies, 2 for 25â€“50%, 3 for 50â€“75%, and 4 for 75â€“100% powdery-mildew coverage.

Under severe adult-plant disease pressure, susceptible genotypes could show colonization of flower sugar leaves, petioles, and stem tissue; adult susceptibility sometimes exceeded the earlier clone-assay result.

PM2 resistance strongly suppressed conidia generation and involved a localized microscopic hypersensitive response without macroscopic chlorotic spots, so symptom-negative or visually clean tissue is not proof that all pathogen interaction is absent.
The scale and response were generated in controlled inoculation and resistance-mapping experiments and are not universal field severity, yield-loss, or intervention thresholds.

Increasing severity can lead to leaf necrosis and defoliation, while high humidity favors infection even though free leaf wetness is not required.

name: Pseudocercospora olive / sooty leaf spot
summary: A Cannabis leaf-spot disease supported by a Thailand field collection and Koch-postulate experiment. Upper-surface olive, gray-centered, or pale vein-limited lesions paired with lower-surface gray-brown sooty sporulation are compatible with Pseudocercospora cannabina, but photographs cannot resolve it from other cercosporoid, fungal, or oomycete diseases. Confirmed labels require plant-linked morphology and molecular evidence.
stages: greenhouse plants near doors or vents
indicators: Natural field symptoms included circular-to-elliptical olive spots with gray centers and dark brown-to-black margins.
Upper-surface lesions can begin as inconspicuous or slight discoloration before becoming pale yellowish, irregular to subcircular, and approximately 2 to 6 mm across.
Lesions may remain bounded by veins, lack a sharply defined margin, and expand across a larger fraction of the leaf.
Corresponding lower-surface areas can be indistinct or pale yellowish rather than matching the upper-surface color exactly.
Grayish-to-pale-brown, velvety or sooty conidial patches occur chiefly on the lower surface and can follow veins.
Magnification may reveal conidiophores emerging in loose fascicles and pale olivaceous-to-pale-brown septate conidia, but morphology must be interpreted by a trained diagnostician.
Severe field disease was associated with defoliation; the institutional handbook also recognizes complete defoliation as a possible outcome.
In a controlled wet-box experiment, lower-surface stomatal penetration occurred within 24 hours and reproduced leaf spots with conidiophores and conidia at 5 days post-inoculation.
exclusions: Dark pinhead pycnidia embedded in lesions support Septoria rather than Pseudocercospora.
Tan-to-white round centers with conspicuous melanized conidiophores and a validated Cercospora result support Cercospora leaf spot.
Purple-to-gray underside growth with angular upper lesions and an oomycete result supports downy mildew.
White superficial colonies that wipe or scrape away and compatible microscopy support powdery mildew rather than a sooty hypophyllous leaf-spot mass.
Concentric rings, black central sporulation, or shot holes can support Alternaria as a differential but still require organism testing.
Mite stippling, webbing, eggs, or mobile mites without lesion-linked fungal structures supports mite injury.
A sharp spray, lamp, aisle, or exposure boundary with no lesion-linked structures supports abiotic contact, light, or chemical injury.
A plant-linked culture or molecular result identifies another organism, or repeated representative lesions fail to yield compatible Pseudocercospora evidence.

progression.description: Upper tissue is inconspicuous to slightly discolored and may already be constrained by veins.
Pale yellowish or olive irregular-to-subcircular lesions become clearer and may reach approximately 2 to 6 mm.
Lower-surface areas remain pale or indistinct while vein-limited gray-brown, velvety-to-sooty conidial masses develop.
Under the reported high-moisture inoculation conditions, penetration was visible at 24 hours and leaf spots with sporulation were reproduced at 5 days.
Lesions can enlarge or cover leaves and affected plants may defoliate; this endpoint is not universal and does not identify the pathogen by itself.

confirmation: Capture the same attached lesion from the upper surface, lower surface, and whole-plant or canopy context; include a scale and record whether lesions follow veins.
Use a hand lens or microscope to determine whether lower-surface dark material is attached conidiophore/conidium growth rather than residue, insects, frass, or necrotic tissue.
Submit multiple representative, actively developing lesions with linked plant and location metadata to a plant diagnostic laboratory; do not base the result on a detached stock image.
Use fungal morphology together with validated sequence evidence; preserve locus, accession, isolate, and sampling details when assigning Pseudocercospora cannabina.
Prefer multilocus evidence such as ITS plus act, tef1, and rpb2 when species resolution matters because type-material sequence data are unavailable and morphology alone is difficult.

Where causality rather than detection is required, retain plant-linked isolation and pathogenicity or equivalent diagnostic evidence; organism detection alone does not prove every lesion was caused by it.

Keep symptom-only, upper-surface-only, detached-leaf-only, mixed-pathogen, unlinked-laboratory, low-resolution, and stock/vendor/forum/generated captures out of the confirmed Pseudocercospora class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Photograph the distribution before removing tissue, then capture matched upper and lower leaf surfaces with a scale.
Preserve several actively sporulating lesions for laboratory diagnosis and limit movement of symptomatic leaves or propagation material.
Record indoor versus field context, greenhouse proximity to open doors or vents, recent wetness, and whether neighboring plants show a clustered or exposure-edge pattern.
correctivePlan: Base sanitation and environmental changes on a confirmed foliar-pathogen diagnosis and applicable local rules.
Track marked lesions and new foliage after intervention; disappearance of leaf wetness or sporulation does not retroactively confirm the species.
Escalate persistent or spreading lesions to a plant diagnostic laboratory rather than repeatedly assigning a visual label.
prevention: Scout both leaf surfaces, especially in field plantings and greenhouse zones near doors or vents.
Improve air circulation, minimize avoidable leaf wetness, and remove infected leaves using sanitary handling.
Reduce carryover of infected crop residue where appropriate because the institutional handbook identifies residue as an overwintering pathway.
warnings: Olive color, gray centers, dark margins, vein limitation, underside growth, and defoliation are compatible features but are not individually or collectively species-specific.

The modern primary evidence is based on twenty symptomatic leaves and two isolates from one Thailand plantation plus one controlled wet-box experiment; cultivar, production-system, geographic, and severity generalization requires more evidence.
The reported 24-hour penetration and 5-day symptom timing came from controlled high-moisture inoculation and must not be treated as a universal field timeline.
Sequence data from Pseudocercospora cannabina type material were unavailable and the broader multilocus clade had weak bootstrap support; species labels need expert morpho-molecular interpretation.

The two CC BY 4.0 figures are mixed composites. They are approved as references but excluded from automated training until panel crops, labels, source grouping, and rights metadata receive human review.
No photograph or video is ground truth without linked sampling and organism evidence; all symptom-only, mixed-organism, unlinked-laboratory, and low-resolution samples require human review.

sources.title: First Molecular Phylogenetic Identification and Report of Pseudocercospora cannabina Causing Leaf Spot Disease on Cannabis sativa in Thailand
supportedClaims: Twenty symptomatic Cannabis leaves were collected from one plantation in Chiang Rai, Thailand, in February 2022; field symptoms were circular-to-elliptical olive leaf spots with gray centers and dark brown-to-black margins, and severely affected plants defoliated.

Upper-surface lesions were initially inconspicuous to slightly discolored and vein-limited, later becoming pale yellowish, irregular to subcircular, approximately 2 to 6 mm, without a distinct margin, and capable of covering the leaf.
Lower-surface lesions were indistinct to pale yellowish and bore hypophyllous, vein-limited, grayish-to-pale-brown, velvety or sooty conidial patches.

In the pathogenicity experiment, hyphae entered through lower-surface stomata within 24 hours, inoculated leaves developed leaf spots at 5 days, water controls remained symptomless, and the reisolate matched the inoculum by morphology and ITS sequence.

Two isolates were identified as Pseudocercospora cannabina using morphology plus ITS, act, tef1, and rpb2 sequence evidence; the authors note missing type-material sequence data and a weakly supported broader phylogenetic clade, limiting visual or single-locus species claims.

Figure 1 is a mixed natural-symptom, whole-canopy, upper/underside, culture, cross-section, conidiophore, and conidium composite; Figure 2 combines controlled lower-surface penetration microscopy with symptom reproduction at 5 days post-inoculation.
The article and its figures are distributed under CC BY 4.0; whole composites still require panel-level review before automated training.

name: Sclerotinia white mold / crown rot complex
summary: A confirmed Cannabis Sclerotinia disease complex that can involve white-mold, crown-rot, wilt, and yellowing syndromes. S. sclerotiorum and S. minor are both documented on Cannabis/hemp; organism-level evidence is required because Botrytis, Fusarium, southern blight, and other molds overlap visually.
affectedParts: leaves or buds at an initial infection site
crown at or near the soil line
shoot and canopy above a girdling canker
indicators: An early attached leaf or bud lesion may look water-soaked before obvious white growth develops; this is a direct institutional hemp observation but is highly nonspecific.
Dry tan-to-brown lesions or cankers develop at the crown or higher on a stem and remain anatomically linked to the declining shoot above them.
Fluffy white or cottony mycelium can cover active stem, crown, or infected bud tissue rather than appearing only as loose material on an uninjured surface.

External sclerotia form within or on the white growth, begin white, and mature black; documented forms range from small irregular bodies in S. minor crown rot to large round, irregular, or ribbon-shaped bodies in S. sclerotiorum stem canker.
A carefully split symptomatic stem may reveal long narrow black sclerotia in the pith or stem cavity, providing a view that superficial mold and residue cannot reproduce.
Wilting and chlorosis can progress to dry foliage, shoot necrosis, or death above a girdling canker while tissue below the lesion is less affected.
Disease position is variable: lower-stem and crown cankers are documented, higher stem cankers occur, and bud rot is possible, but the Oregon primary report observed no flower infection.

A confirmed species label requires plant-linked isolation or microscopy plus molecular evidence and, in primary reports, symptom reproduction and reisolation; sclerotial appearance alone does not resolve species.
exclusions: Gray-to-brown sporulation dominates rotting buds or stems and plant-linked testing identifies Botrytis cinerea rather than Sclerotinia.
A basal lesion in warm conditions carries abundant mustard-seed-sized tan-to-brown sclerotia and testing identifies the southern-blight pathogen rather than Sclerotinia.
Internal vascular browning, root/crown testing, culture, or molecular results support Fusarium wilt or crown rot.
Roots are water-soaked or cortex-sloughed and oomycete testing supports Pythium or another water mold without a Sclerotinia canker and sclerotia.
The white material is a superficial powdery-mildew colony without a stem canker, cottony internal growth, or sclerotia.
The material wipes or dissolves as mineral, spray, fiber, webbing, or other nonliving residue and the underlying tissue lacks a compatible active lesion.
Black structures are pycnidia embedded in a Diaporthe or other stem lesion, or magnification shows insect frass rather than fungal sclerotia.
Only nonspecific wilt, senescence, dead debris, or unlinked white growth is visible and no active lesion margin, attached canker, sclerotium, or organism evidence accompanies it.

progression.description: Wet, senescing, wounded, or infected leaf or bud tissue provides context for infection, but environmental history alone is not a positive label.
A water-soaked leaf or bud lesion or a localized tan stem lesion develops at an attached infection site; serial close-ups should preserve its position.
The lesion expands into a crown or stem canker and fluffy white mycelium becomes visible on active tissue; decline begins above a constricting lesion.
Sclerotia form white and mature black externally, or long narrow black bodies become visible inside a split stem; form varies by species and site.
A girdled shoot, crown, or infected bud dries and dies while mature sclerotia remain in or on tissue and can persist after the visible canopy collapses.

lookAlikes: Botrytis gray mold or bud rot
Rhizoctonia sore shin or root rot
Mechanical stem split, abrasion, or sunscald
Nonliving spray, mineral, fiber, or web residue
Caterpillar or other bud injury with secondary decay
confirmation: Capture the same plant as a whole, the exact shoot-to-canker connection, the lesion margin, and the crown or bud site with a scale; retain canopy position, crop stage, cultivar, date, and production setting.

Mark the lesion and make repeated images before disturbance to document water soaking, canker expansion, white growth, sclerotial color change, and whether decline remains anatomically above the lesion.
Record whether the lesion is at the soil-contact crown, lower stem, upper stem, or bud and inspect adjacent leaves and buds; do not require flower symptoms when a stem canker is present.

When safe and diagnostically appropriate, split a representative symptomatic stem longitudinally and photograph the pith and any internal sclerotia with scale, keeping it linked to exterior and whole-plant views.
Submit an active lesion margin and representative sclerotia to a plant diagnostic laboratory for microscopy and culture; sample before disposal or a treatment obscures signs.
Use validated molecular evidence to resolve Sclerotinia and species; the Oregon report combined ITS and G3PDH data with phylogeny, pathogenicity, symptom reproduction, and reisolation.

Route symptom-only, detached, species-inferred, unlinked-laboratory, mixed-pathogen, low-resolution, rights-unclear, forum, vendor, stock, or generated images and videos to human review rather than confirmed ground truth.
immediateActions: Photograph the plant-to-lesion connection and preserve fresh lesion-margin and sclerotial material before moving or discarding the plant.
Clearly mark or separate suspect plants where operationally appropriate and avoid moving wet symptomatic tissue through unaffected crop areas.
Record recent wetness, irrigation, condensation, canopy closure, wounds, senescing tissue, crop stage, lesion height, and whether symptoms occur in a spatial cluster.
correctivePlan: Base disease management on a plant-linked laboratory result and measures legal and appropriate for the crop, jurisdiction, and production system.
Remove confirmed infected material and sclerotia using sanitary handling appropriate to the site; clean tools and surfaces to avoid moving contaminated debris.
Reduce avoidable extended tissue wetness and improve drying or airflow where feasible, while recognizing that environmental response does not retrospectively confirm Sclerotinia.
prevention: Scout crowns, stem junctions, senescing leaves, and dense flower sites during prolonged wetness, preserving external and internal views when a canker is found.
Limit carryover of infected plant debris and sclerotia and maintain sanitation for tools, containers, floors, and production areas appropriate to the system.
Keep cultivar, field or room zone, irrigation, canopy-wetness, wound, and prior-disease metadata so recurrent site patterns can be evaluated.
warnings: Photo/video-only confidence is capped at 0.30: even white mycelium plus black structures requires verification that the structures are sclerotia on the same actively diseased plant.
Sclerotinia sclerotiorum and S. minor overlap visually and must not be separated by canopy appearance, sclerotial size, shape, or infection position alone.
Water-soaked lesions, white cottony growth, cankers, wilt, and shoot death each overlap Botrytis, southern blight, Fusarium, Pythium, bacterial decay, injury, and residue.
Bud infection is documented by institutional guidance but was absent from the Oregon stem-canker report; it is possible, not required, and must not be inferred from a stem-only view.
Exact wetness duration, temperature, disease timing, incidence, and economic loss from one site or experiment are contextual observations rather than universal Cannabis thresholds.

The three institutional hemp images below have no explicit item-level reuse or automated-training permission. They are hidden metadata references, no media file is copied, and all remain training-prohibited.
No verified diagnostic video or controlled same-plant progression sequence was located; every symptom-only, detached, unlinked, mixed-organism, or rights-unclear sample requires human review.
Sclerotinia sclerotiorum and S. minor should not be separated by canopy appearance alone; crown signs, sclerotia, culture, and molecular evidence carry more weight.

sources.title: Emerging Fungal and Oomycete Diseases of Cannabis in South Africa: First Reports and Pathogenicity Confirmation
supportedClaims: Cannabis samples from an aeroponic facility with wilting, yellowing, white mold, and gray mold were investigated with DNA sequence data and pathogenicity testing.

Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, Botrytis cinerea, Fusarium oxysporum, and Pythium myriotylum were all confirmed capable of causing disease, demonstrating strong visual overlap among mold and wilt syndromes.
Sclerotinia diagnosis therefore requires organism-level evidence rather than white mold appearance alone.

sources.title: First Report of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum Causing Stem Canker on Cannabis sativa in Oregon
supportedClaims: At two Oregon hoop-house hemp farms, affected plants developed wilting and chlorosis followed by shoot necrosis, with dry tan-to-brown stem lesions or cankers, white mycelium, and large black round, irregular, or ribbon-shaped sclerotia.
Cankers occurred at the crown and higher on stems; flowers were not infected in this report, so visible bud involvement is not required for a stem-canker diagnosis.

ITS and G3PDH sequence evidence, phylogenetic analysis, pathogenicity testing, symptom reproduction, and reisolation supported Sclerotinia sclerotiorum as the cause; appearance alone did not establish the species.
The observations came from two farms in one season and the report states that economic impact was unclear, so incidence and loss must not be generalized.

supportedClaims: The institutional hemp guide, revised March 2026, describes water-soaked lesions on leaves or buds as a usual first symptom, followed by stem invasion near infected buds, upper-shoot death, or lower-stem cankers.

Active stems and buds may become whitish from fluffy white mycelium; sclerotia can form externally or inside stems, begin white, mature black, and include long narrow internal forms visible after splitting a stem.

name: Septoria leaf spot complex
summary: A lower- and inner-canopy hemp leaf-spot syndrome caused by Septoria species. Dark pycnidia within expanding brown-gray lesions are useful evidence, but modern work shows more than one Septoria species can infect Cannabis.
indicators: Disease often begins on lower or inner-canopy leaves
Small irregular brown-to-gray spots expand to several millimeters
Dark round pycnidia can be visible within lesions
Older leaves may defoliate as disease advances
exclusions: Sooty conidial masses on the underside support Pseudocercospora
White-centered round lesions with a pronounced dark border support Cercospora as a differential
Shot-hole lesions and Colletotrichum evidence support anthracnose
No fungal structures or lab evidence are present and an abiotic exposure fits the distribution better

progression.description: Small discolored spots appear on older or inner leaves.
Brown-to-gray lesions enlarge and reproductive structures may become visible.
Lesions multiply and older foliage can yellow and drop.

confirmation: Examine lesions for pycnidia and submit representative tissue for fungal identification when species matters.
Use morphology and molecular sequence data for species-level Septoria classification because S. cannabis and S. cannabicola cannot be separated by a generic spot photo.
immediateActions: Document lower-versus-upper canopy distribution and both leaf surfaces.
Limit movement of symptomatic foliage into clean production areas.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed-disease sanitation and environmental management appropriate to the system.
Track new lesion development after intervention.
prevention: Scout lower and inner canopy foliage early.
Reduce prolonged leaf wetness and carryover of infected debris where practical.
warnings: Septoria species taxonomy on Cannabis is not reducible to visual symptoms.
Do not train a species classifier from mixed Septoria figures without organism-confirmed labels.

sources.title: Reemergence of Septoria Leaf Spot Caused by Septoria cannabis on Hemp in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Septoria leaf spot was documented on hemp primarily on lower leaves and inner canopy, with small irregular brown-to-gray lesions expanding to roughly 5 to 7.5 mm and dark pycnidia in lesions.
Eight isolates were tested for pathogenicity on greenhouse-grown hemp and diagnostic loci were sequenced; morphology and sequence evidence supported Septoria cannabis in the Kentucky material.
Visual lesion appearance alone cannot separate Septoria from other hemp leaf-spot pathogens.

sources.title: Septoria cannabicola, a new species on Cannabis sativa from Japan
supportedClaims: Molecular phylogeny and morphology demonstrated that Cannabis leaf spot historically attributed to Septoria cannabis can involve a distinct species, Septoria cannabicola.
Natural symptoms began as indistinct yellow spots on lower leaves and progressed to brown irregular lesions and premature defoliation of older leaves.
Species-level Septoria naming therefore requires laboratory evidence rather than lesion appearance alone.

sources.title: Leaf Spot Disease Development and Its Effect on Yield of Essential Oil-Producing Hemp Cultivars in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Two Kentucky field experiments in 2020 and 2021 evaluated Bipolaris, Cercospora, and Septoria leaf spots across four essential-oil hemp cultivar groups.
In those experiments Bipolaris was first observed seven to eight weeks after planting and increased through the end of the season; this is a study observation, not a universal onset rule.
All three evaluated leaf spots were more severe in the middle canopy than the upper canopy, and susceptibility differed among cultivar groups; neither pattern is a universal diagnostic threshold.
Reported yield associations concerned the combined leaf-spot disease complex under the tested cultivars, sites, and seasons and must not be attributed to Bipolaris alone.
Overlapping leaf-spot syndromes mean paired canopy observations, temporal follow-up, fungal morphology, culture, and molecular diagnostics are more reliable than one lesion photograph.

name: Southern blight
summary: A warm-condition soilborne Cannabis disease centered at the soil line, crown and taproot. White cottony mycelium plus tan-to-brown spherical sclerotia at the plant base are strong signs, but wilt alone is nonspecific.
indicators: Dark brown-to-tan discoloration develops near the soil line
Rot extends into crown or taproot while foliage yellows and the plant wilts/collapses
White cottony mycelium develops on basal tissue or adjacent soil
Numerous spherical tan-to-dark-brown sclerotia occur with compatible basal rot
exclusions: No basal rot, mycelium or sclerotia are present and measured drought explains wilt
Laboratory evidence identifies Rhizoctonia, Fusarium, Pythium or another root/crown pathogen
White growth is confined to leaves/flowers without basal disease

progression.description: Dark tan-brown discoloration appears at the soil line.
Rot moves into crown and taproot as foliage yellows.
Whole plants can wilt and collapse while white mycelium and brown sclerotia accumulate at the base.

confirmation: Inspect the soil line/crown/root surface for characteristic mycelium and sclerotia and submit tissue/culture for organism confirmation.
Record temperature/moisture context, but do not use hot wet conditions as diagnostic proof.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone material and prevent movement of contaminated soil or debris to clean areas.
Preserve basal tissue and sclerotia for diagnostic testing.
correctivePlan: Use confirmed soilborne-disease sanitation and crop-legal management appropriate to the setting.
Address excess moisture where measured without assuming moisture correction eliminates established pathogen inoculum.
prevention: Avoid moving contaminated soil or plant debris between production areas.
Monitor crown/root health during warm wet periods.
warnings: Whole-plant wilt alone cannot identify southern blight.
Sclerotia and laboratory evidence are substantially stronger than canopy appearance.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017â€“2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

The survey documented Serratia-associated, vein-limited angular hemp lesions and red bacterial ooze emerging from punctured lesions, while emphasizing that hemp leaf diseases overlap visually and require diagnostic separation.

sources.title: First Report of Southern Blight Caused by Sclerotium rolfsii on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Sicily and Southern Italy
supportedClaims: Infected hemp developed dark brown-to-tan discoloration at the soil line, crown and taproot rot, foliar yellowing, whole-plant collapse, white cottony mycelium, and tan-to-dark-brown spherical sclerotia.
Pathogenicity was reproduced on hemp and Sclerotium rolfsii was reisolated while noninoculated controls remained symptomless.
High summer temperatures and high soil moisture were associated with the reported outbreak but are risk context, not diagnostic proof.

name: Stable chlorotic sectoring / suspected genetic variegation
summary: Sharply bounded chlorotic or chlorophyll-deficient sectors can be consistent with somatic mutation or mosaicism in Cannabis, but no published Cannabis image morphology proves genetic cause; treat this as an exclusion-based phenotype until serial lineage evidence and appropriate laboratory work support the attribution.
affectedParts: successive leaves from one shoot or meristem
whole plant only when a documented cultivar trait is established
stages: flowering; stage specificity is not established
indicators: Abrupt yellow, cream, pale-green, or near-white tissue adjoining normally green tissue within the same leaf
Sector-shaped or longitudinal pigment loss rather than uniform whole-leaf yellowing
The same shoot position or clonal lineage is mapped across successive leaves and time rather than inferred from one detached leaf
Affected tissue retains its boundary while new observations document whether the pattern remains localized, expands, disappears, or is joined by distortion and stunting
Matched images preserve upper and lower leaf surfaces, whole-plant distribution, branch identity, scale, cultivar, developmental stage, and camera-lighting conditions
exclusions: Validated testing detects a virus or viroid consistent with the sampled tissue and syndrome
Mosaic, mottling, line patterns, curling, brittle growth, shortened internodes, stunting, or reduced inflorescence performance progress beyond the original sector
Chlorosis follows leaf age, interveinal or marginal patterns, or a measured tissue-nutrient, substrate-pH, or root-zone-EC abnormality better than a branch lineage
Microscopy or organism sampling confirms thrips, mites, leafminers, or another pest associated with the marks
The distribution maps to a lamp, spray, pesticide, plant-growth regulator, abrasion, heat event, or other documented exposure
Camera white balance, glare, shadow, senescence, or cultivar pigmentation explains the apparent color boundary

progression.description: Capture calibrated whole-plant, branch, upper-surface, and lower-surface views; assign a symptom-only chlorotic-sector label, not a genetic ground-truth label.

Mark the shoot and record successive leaves and any cuttings over time. A stable lineage association increases suspicion of a developmental or genetic origin but does not exclude latent or localized infection.
Compare matched healthy tissue and evaluate pests, root-zone pH and EC, nutrient status, exposure history, and a region- and facility-appropriate virus/viroid panel before narrowing the cause.

Use genetic or meristem-lineage analysis when a genetic claim matters. Cannabis somatic mosaicism has been sequenced within one mother plant, but published evidence does not establish a universal visible phenotype or inheritance rule.

lookAlikes: Mosaic, mottling, or line-pattern syndrome of unresolved cause
Lettuce chlorosis virus or other regional virus
Iron, manganese, magnesium, or nitrogen disorder
Camera color, glare, or shadow artifact
confirmation: Do not confirm genetic variegation, chimerism, mutation, virus freedom, or training ground truth from a photograph or video.
Record the exact leaf, node, branch, plant, cultivar, propagation source, date, stage, lighting, and serial change; include healthy plants of the same cultivar and environment.
Inspect both leaf surfaces and protected growth with magnification, and document pest organisms or their absence separately from the color phenotype.

Measure root-zone pH and EC and review irrigation, tissue or solution analysis, nutrient history, spray records, lamp position, temperature, and mechanical injury before assigning a developmental explanation.

Submit symptomatic and matched asymptomatic tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory for a locally appropriate validated virus/viroid differential; a negative targeted assay excludes only the agents and sample covered by that assay.
When a genetic attribution is operationally important, compare mapped sectors and clones and use qualified genetic or meristem-lineage analysis; persistence alone is supportive context, not proof.
immediateActions: Keep the visual label at â€œchlorotic sectoringâ€”cause unresolvedâ€ and flag it for human review.
Pause distribution of suspect cuttings and separate them from verified genetic-trait references until infectious causes are reasonably excluded.
Preserve serial imagery and matched tissue before pruning or discarding the affected shoot.
correctivePlan: Correct only measured root-zone, nutrient, pest, or exposure problems and document whether new growth changes.
If validated pathogen testing is positive, move the sample to the confirmed pathogen class and follow the facilityâ€™s sanitation and plant-health protocol.
If differential testing is negative and the pattern tracks a shoot or clone, retain a â€œsuspected genetic/developmentalâ€ label unless genetic evidence supports a stronger claim.
prevention: Maintain cultivar, mother-plant, cutting-position, and clone-lineage records.
Use tested propagation stock and tool-sanitation practices so a stable-looking pattern is not assumed noninfectious.
Capture healthy reference plants under repeatable lighting and camera settings for color comparison.
warnings: â€œGenetic mosaicismâ€ describes within-organism genetic variation; a visible â€œmosaic symptomâ€ is not evidence of that mechanism.
The Cannabis mosaicism sequencing study sampled one mother plant and did not link its variants to visible leaf sectors.
The VIGS bleaching experiment was an intentionally virus-vector-induced gene-silencing phenotype and must not be treated as proof that natural bleaching is inherited or noninfectious.

The composite reference image mixes four unresolved mosaic-like presentations with panel e, which the authors characterize as somatic-mutation-associated chlorotic sectors; preserve panel labels and never train the entire composite as one genetic class.
Negative molecular, microscopy, or indicator-host findings are bounded by sample quality, agent coverage, assay performance, and observation time.
This reviewed record validates an uncertainty-bounded workflow, not image-only genetic ground truth; all symptom-only samples remain human-review items.

sources.title: Accumulation of somatic mutations leads to genetic mosaicism in cannabis
sources.publisher: Wiley on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America
supportedClaims: Deep whole-genome sequencing of top, middle, and bottom samples from one 1.5-year-old Cannabis mother plant detected many variants unique to individual canopy samples, demonstrating within-plant genetic mosaicism in that plant.
The study examined a single mother plant and did not validate a visible leaf-sector pattern as a diagnostic marker of somatic mutation, heritability, or clonal stability.

sources.title: Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Experimental silencing of Cannabis phytoene desaturase and magnesium-chelatase-subunit-I genes produced spotted leaf bleaching, 70â€“73% lower target-transcript expression, and corresponding carotenoid or chlorophyll-a reductions.

This deliberately induced, virus-vector phenotype shows that perturbing pigment-related gene expression can create visible bleaching; it does not establish that naturally occurring sectors are genetic or safe from infectious differentials.

sources.title: Challenges to Cannabis sativa Production from Pathogens and Microbesâ€”The Role of Molecular Diagnostics and Bioinformatics
sources.organization: International Journal of Molecular Sciences (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: The authors documented Cannabis leaves with mosaic, mottling, and line patterns that superficially resembled viral symptoms, and separately illustrated sharply chlorotic, chlorophyll-deficient sectors attributed to somatic mutation in Figure 4e.

Defined broad-spectrum and specific RT-PCR assays did not detect the targeted viruses in tested OG Kush and Headband tissues; positive controls worked, no virus-like particles were seen in the examined Cannabis samples by transmission electron microscopy, and inoculated indicator hosts remained symptomless for three weeks.

Those negative results apply only to the sampled tissues, agents, assays, and observation period and therefore do not establish genetic causality or exclude every virus, viroid, pest, nutrient, root-zone, or chemical cause.

media.caption: Rights-cleared reference composite from the author preprint corresponding to the peer-reviewed Punja et al. paper. Only panel e is presented by the authors as somatic-mutation-associated chlorotic sectoring; panels aâ€“d are visually overlapping, unresolved mosaic-like differentials. It is not genetic ground truth.

Figure 4 in the 2023 Preprints.org version of â€œChallenges to Cannabis sativa Production from Pathogens and Microbesâ€”the Role of Molecular Diagnostics and Bioinformatics,â€ CC BY 4.0; link the source and license and indicate any modification.

useLimitations: Reference URL only; the asset is not copied into the repository.
Panel e is the suspected somatic-mutation comparison; panels aâ€“d are unresolved mosaic-like differentials and must not inherit the genetic label.
No panel is sequence-confirmed as the cause shown; retain panel labels, caption context, and human review.
CC BY permits automated use with attribution, but this composite is excluded from training eligibility because its panels contain different and incompletely resolved labels.
